chronic atrial fibrillation (AF), a common arrhythmia, has a major impact on mortality.
the mortality risk in patients with chronic atrial fibrillation (CAF) remains high despite advances in treatment.

(1) AF is an independent risk factor for mortality; (2) rhythm control strategies have not been shown to be superior to rate control strategies; (3) the risk of mortality in AF patients is due to the associated comorbidities and complications of the arrhythmia; (4) novel oral anti-coagulents have been shown to be more efficacious in reducing mortality than warfarin.

the epidemiological and clinical features of AF-related morbidity and mortality and the likely impact of novel anti-arrhythmatic drugs and anti-coagulatns upon mortality reduction in the future.
the epidemiological aspects of chronic atrial fibrillation and the impact of novel anticoagulants upon the associated mortality.
the epidemiology of chronic atrial fibrillation and its impact on mortality in the modern treatment era.

chronic AF is associated with increased mortality, but that mortality is not solely due to the arrhythmia but rather due to a combination of factors.
the burden of mortality due to AF is still high and that novel anti-coagulant strategies may have a role to play in the near future.

the mortality risk associated with AF is due to a combination of the associated co-morbidity, the embolic risk and the side-effects of treatment.

AF-related mortality is still a significant public health concern and that novel anti-coagulant therapies will be a key determinant in the future management of AF and its associated mortality.
